title: Rethinking Klebsiella pneumoniae vaccines: from protective immunity to rational vaccine design
abstract:
Nature Communications, Published online: 24 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79574-7

This Review highlights barriers to cross-protective Klebsiella pneumoniae vaccines and proposes a paradigm shift, integrating antigen discovery, systems immunology and translational models to define conserved protective targets and immune correlates.

title: Quantum physics can prove where you are
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03378-4

Demonstrating your location to someone far away is surprisingly hard. Quantum correlations offer a way to do so without needing to trust any quantum hardware.

title: Pre-rRNA represses gene transcription in the XY body of male germ cells
abstract: Nucleolus is disassembled when the nuclear envelope breaks down during mitosis prophase. However, the dynamics of nucleolus in meiotic prophase remain unclear. Here, by tracking nucleolar components of spermatocytes in mice, we show that the nucleolus is fragmented even before the breakdown of the nuclear envelope. Instead of dissolving in nucleoplasm or cytoplasm, the nucleolar components are reaggregated and fused with the XY body during prophase I of meiosis. The dynamic relocation of the nucleolar components to the XY body is governed by the ATR-dependent signaling pathway. Moreover, the relocated pre-ribosomal RNA (pre-rRNA) covers the entire X and Y chromosomes. The treatment with RNA polymerase I inhibitor BMH-21 only disrupts the accumulation of pre-rRNA but not other nucleolar components on the X and Y chromosomes. title: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03602-1

Global agricultural demand has increased over the past few decades, driving land-use intensification in some of the world’s most biodiverse regions. An assessment of some 40,000 species, from soil microorganisms to vertebrates, in Sumatra, Indonesia, reveals that agricultural intensification threatens biodiversity through species loss and changes in community composition across different spatial scales.

title: Rethinking corporate climate targets for real-world transitions
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11100-7

Frameworks for corporate greenhouse gas reduction targets should place greater emphasis on systemic changes in business models, technologies and value chains; the scientific community has a role in developing robust, actionable frameworks for corporate decarbonization.

title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies
abstract:
Nature, Published online: 18 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11284-y

A basin-wide assessment of Amazonian deciduousness using high-resolution satellite observations shows a diverse range of phenological strategies across the Amazon rainforest, contrary to the prevailing view of Amazonian phenology.

title: Rethinking laboratory sustainability
abstract: Green lab initiatives like My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), are paving the way towards sustainable research by promoting resource efficiency, energy conservation, and waste reduction through behavioral changes. However, these initiatives focus almost exclusively on material consumption, overlooking deeper facets of scientific waste that stem from questionable research practices: the environmental cost of unnecessary or poorly designed experiments, discarded null results, unreproducible research, and distorted reporting. I argue that a more meaningful discussion of scientific sustainability must look beyond physical resource management to examine the scientific process itself; to rethink the questions we ask, the experiments we do, and how we communicate our findings. title: Winding-up of fibrin fibers as a novel mechanism of platelet-mediated fiber compaction
abstract: This study reveals an unrecognized mechanism by which platelets retract and compact fibrin fibers. Using a newly developed 2D fiber-retraction assay, we observed a ‘gearwheel’ pattern of actomyosin in spread platelets with associated, extracellular fibrin patches that appear to initiate fibrin fiber attachment and rearrangement. The outcome of this process results in two morphologically different platelet populations. Spread platelets with coiled fibers around and above their pseudo-nucleus. Other, only partially spread platelets have tightly packed fibers around bulbous protrusions (‘bulbs’), mirroring the architecture of platelets and adjacent fibers within a retracted clot. Thus, the observed compaction process might take place during clot retraction to reduce clot volume, stiffen the clot, and enhance wound repair. title: Efficacy of erector spinae plane block for patients with inflammatory bowel disease undergoing major abdominal surgery: A double-blind randomized controlled trial
abstract:
by Yasmin Alhamdah, Yehoshua Gleicher, Hermann dos Santos Fernandes, Sharon Peacock, Xiang Y. Ye, Christopher Brown, Anthony de Buck van Overstraeten, Zeev Friedman, Naveed Siddiqui

Objectives

Patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) undergoing abdominal surgery face challenges in postoperative recovery due to high opioid needs and limited analgesic alternatives. The erector spinae plane (ESP) block has been shown to improve recovery in abdominal procedures, but its efficacy in the IBD population remains unknown. We investigated whether bilateral ESP blocks improve postoperative quality of recovery in this population.

Methods

In this prospective, double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized trial, adults with IBD scheduled for elective laparoscopic-assisted abdominal surgery were randomized to receive bilateral ESP blocks with either 0.5% ropivacaine or normal saline before induction of anesthesia. title: When should adaptation arise from a polygenic response versus few large-effect changes?
abstract:
by William R. Milligan, Laura K. Hayward, Guy Sella

When will adaptation involve a few genetic changes of large effect versus a polygenic response? There are compelling reasons to expect polygenic adaptation to be common, yet direct evidence is lacking. Conversely, there are hundreds of examples of large-effect adaptations across species, but it is unclear whether they occur frequently within any given species. These different lines of evidence are hard to synthesize, in part due to the lack of theory that relates them. To address this gap, we frame the question in terms of the properties of an adaptive trait. We ask how the genetic basis of adaptation depends on key aspects of genetic variation in the trait and on the degree to which its selection pressures have changed. To this end, we consider a quantitative trait subject to stabilizing selection and model its response when a population at mutation–selection–drift balance experiences a sudden shift in the trait optimum. title: GEI-17-mediated SUMOylation of GDP dissociation inhibitor GDI-1 regulates apoptotic cell clearance
abstract:
by Lei Yuan, Peiyao Li, Aiying Ma, Chao Li, Fuqiao Liu, Yunmin Xie, Qian Zheng, Hui Wang, Hui Xiao

Apoptotic cell clearance represents the final stage of apoptosis and involves phagosome formation, maturation, and digestion. Here, we found that SUMO modifications participate in apoptotic cell clearance by influencing phagosomal degradation activity in C. elegans. The SUMO E3 ligase, GEI-17, SUMOylates GDP dissociation inhibitor (GDI-1) at K270 to trigger phagosomal degradation. Upon SUMOylation, GDI-1 facilitates release of GDP-bound RAB-1, which is subsequently converted to the GTP-bound form in a manner dependent on GDI displacement factor, PRAF-3. RAB-1 conversion enables binding and translocation of RAB-7 from the endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to promote phagosome maturation and degradation activity. title: Local feedback governs cell fate transition to drive self-organized phenotypic equilibrium in hierarchical tumors
abstract:
by Emma Legait, Charlotte Rulquin, Lauranne Bouteille, Raphaël Clément, Cédric Maurange

How cell-state transitions are regulated along a tumor lineage to determine its overall cellular composition remains unclear. Using a simple hierarchical tumor model in Drosophila, we show that differentiation of cancer stem cells (CSCs) into transit amplifying progenitors (TAPs) depends on the fraction of TAPs among their immediate neighbors. This relationship is captured by a local feedback transition rule that quantitatively predicts CSC transition probability. Implementing this rule in 3D growth simulations spontaneously recapitulates CSC clustering and the emergence of a stable CSC fraction within tumors. Mechanistically, the local feedback is mediated by EGFR signaling from newly produced TAPs, propagating differentiation across CSC clusters. title: Dynamic functional connectivity reveals evolving neural activity states of alcohol-seeking in rats
abstract:
by Yujing Zhang, Nicholas M. Timme, Mintao Liu, Christopher C. Lapish, Joaquín Goñi

The brain mechanisms underlying persistent alcohol-seeking in Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) remain incompletely understood. To investigate this behavior, we characterized the temporal evolution of neural activity states in the anterior cingulate cortex of freely behaving rats performing an aversion-resistant drinking (ARD) task. Alcohol-preferring (P) rats were assessed, as they reliably exhibit ARD when alcohol is devalued with the bitter tastant quinine. P rats were compared with Wistar rats, which progress slower to ARD, as indicated by cessation of drinking following quinine devaluation. Using dynamic functional connectivity analyses of spike-train recordings, we identified latent neural states corresponding to seeking and non-seeking phases. title: Economic value of gonorrhea resistance testing in the United States: A multi-perspective modeling study
abstract:
by Brooke E. Nichols, Betsy Wonderly Trainor, Grace Hampson, Yonatan H. Grad, Jeffrey D. Klausner

Background

Rising antimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae threatens the effectiveness of existing therapies. Ceftriaxone is the only recommended first-line (empiric) treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea in the United States. Ciprofloxacin is no longer recommended for empiric use because of widespread resistance, but it is inexpensive, taken orally, and effective against susceptible infections, which a resistance test can identify. In the context of rising resistance, resistance-guided treatment (RGT) may reduce treatment failures, complications, and inappropriate use of last-line agents while slowing resistance emergence and preserving the efficacy of new and existing drugs. title: The state of genetic literacy among high school students in Czechia
abstract:
by Marek Procházka, Markéta Klimešová, Vanda Janštová

To investigate high school students’ understanding of modern genetics and to characterize the obstacles that impede deeper understanding of this subject, we translated the Learning Progression‑Based Assessment of Modern Genetics diagnostic instrument into Czech and validated it with 282 Czech high school students. We present the Czech version of this instrument which spans Mendelian genetics; molecular biology (proteins, nucleic acids, gene expression); mutation; cell division; genetics–evolution connections; environmental influences on phenotype; intra‑individual and inter‑individual genetic variation; and interspecific differences. Czech high school students frequently fail to connect proteins to phenotypic traits, rarely attain molecular‑level reasoning, and underappreciate the evolutionary significance of genetic mechanisms. title: Associations of physical exercise and sedentary behavior with problematic smartphone use and interaction anxiety in a predominantly first-year convenience sample of Chinese college students: A cross-sectional study
abstract:
by Qi Han

Problematic smartphone use and interaction anxiety are common concerns in university settings, but their joint relationships with exercise and sedentary behavior remain unclear. We examined these associations in a predominantly first-year convenience sample recruited through 36 universities in four Chinese provinces. The analytical sample included 1,025 students aged 18 years or older, of whom 902 (88.0%) were first-year students. Physical exercise was represented by an adapted self-reported exercise-volume index derived from exercise intensity, duration, and frequency. Sedentary behavior was assessed with a single item whose response categories used inconsistent daily and weekly time frames; it was therefore analyzed as an exploratory categorical indicator. Problematic smartphone use and interaction anxiety were measured with the 22-item Smartphone Addiction Scale for College Students and the conventionally scored 15-item Interaction Anxiousness Scale. title: Ten-year clinical outcomes after successful percutaneous coronary intervention compared with medical treatment in patients with chronic total occlusion and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction
abstract:
by Hye Yon Yu, Jihun Ahn, Seung-Woon Rha, Byoung Geol Choi, Se Yeon Choi, Jae Kyeong Byun, Youjin Lee, Abiseka Panji Baskoro, Aditya Reza Pratama, Melly Susanti, Manda Satria Chesario, Soohyung Park, Cheol Ung Choi

Background

The long-term clinical benefit of revascularization in patients with chronic total occlusion (CTO) and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF ≥50%) remains uncertain.

Purpose

This study aimed to investigate the clinical impact of CTO revascularization in patients with preserved LVEF compared with those receiving optimal medical treatment (OMT) up to 10 years.

Methods

A total of 939 patients with CTO and preserved LVEF were analyzed, including those treated with OMT (OMT group; n = 492) or successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI group; n = 447). title: Developmental bias explains the evolutionary trend towards simple leaf shapes
abstract: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. title: Loss to follow-up during tuberculosis treatment and 5-year mortality in Brazil: A target trial emulation
abstract:
by Evelyn Lepka de Lima, Ana Angélica Lindoso, Giovanna Mariah Orlandi, Suely Fukasava, Catia Martinez, Julio Croda, C. Robert Horsburgh Jr., Otavio Ranzani, Meredith B. Brooks, Jason R. Andrews

Background

Loss to follow-up (LTFU) during tuberculosis treatment is a major programmatic gap, but how much excess mortality it causes has been difficult to estimate, because individuals who disengage differ from those who do not, and they must survive long enough to be recorded as having disengaged. Quantifying this excess and identifying which populations are at greatest risk are critical to informing program design and resource allocation.
